newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's centersouth expects bumper sugar crop.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's centersouth expects bumper sugar crop.

text.p: Brazil's centersouth sugar producing region should achieve a 1996/97 sugar output some ten percent up on 1995/96's 9.27 million tonnes, said the Sao Paulo State Sugar and Alcohol Producers' Association AIAA.

The region's total alcohol production is meanwhile expected to be 11.9 billion liters, up from 1995/96's 10.8 billion, and out of a total foreseen for the whole of Brazil of 13.8 billion liters this year under the government's current sugar crop plan.
"We'll have a better sugar harvest than for several years," said an AIAA corporate affairs spokesman. "This is mainly due to this year's exceptionally good climatic conditions."
The spokesman said rains before the start of the sugarcane harvest followed by dry weather during harvesting in the May-August period, had favored crop size and yield.
The favorable crop weather conditions are expected to continue in the states of Sao Paulo, Parana, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Goias, Rio de Janeiro and Espirito Santo.

Sugar harvesting and crushing in the region started as early as April this year, due to both the favorable weather conditions and fears of a domestic market shortage of anhydrous alcohol, the AIAA spokesman said.
Harvesting can be expected to continue until October or November, he said.
Up to September 1, AIAA had registered an output of 6.49 million tonnes of sugar in the centresouth, 25.17 percent above the same time last year.
Total alcohol production was also up 21 percent on the same date in 1995, at 7.54 billion liters.

The AIAA spokesman said that despite the firm indications of increased production this year, there have so far been no negotiations between industry and government on the possibility of increasing sugar export quotas.
This year's sugar crop plan limits sugar exports from the centersouth region to around 3.7 million tonnes, similar to in 1995, AIAA said.
Exports above this level are subject to payment of a 40 percent tax on the fob export price unless extra export quotas can be negotiated with the government, the spokesman said.
Continuing firm restrictions on sugar exports could lead to downwards pressure on domestic sugar prices, he said.
-- Diana Kinch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
